claims.text: Post-synthesis femtosecond laser irradiation induces rapid localized atomic ordering in near-equiatomic multielement nanoparticles.
Post-synthesis femtosecond laser irradiation anneals defects in these nanoparticles.
Laser-induced ordering and defect annealing retard diffusion during subsequent high-temperature service.
Laser-induced ordering and defect annealing retard phase separation during high-temperature service.
Laser-treated nanoparticles retain structural and chemical stability better than untreated nanoparticles during catalytic or thermoelectric operation.
The as-synthesized nanoparticles are atomically disordered, defect-rich, and lattice-distorted.
Femtosecond pulsed laser irradiation can be applied after nanoparticle synthesis with controlled fluence and pulse duration.
The relevant service ranges are 773–1173 K for catalysis and 473–1923 K for thermoelectrics.
Femtosecond laser pulses deposit energy into the nanoparticle lattice over a few picoseconds.
Because lattice energy deposition is much faster than heat transfer to the surroundings, femtosecond irradiation produces nearly adiabatic localized heating.
The transient laser-induced heating increases metal-atom diffusion during irradiation.
Laser-enhanced diffusion is limited enough to anneal defects and induce short-range order rather than causing extensive restructuring.
Greater atomic ordering lowers the diffusion coefficient during later high-temperature exposure.
Greater atomic ordering reduces the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation.
The laser-induced ordered structure is both thermodynamically and kinetically stabilized.
Untreated nanoparticles retain greater disorder and higher defect density than laser-treated nanoparticles.
Untreated nanoparticles undergo faster diffusion and phase separation during high-temperature exposure than laser-treated nanoparticles.
Laser fluence and pulse duration must remain below conditions that cause complete melting or unwanted morphological transformation.
Excessive laser exposure can trigger deleterious phase changes or phase segregation.
The optimal laser-processing window and the quantitative relationship between induced ordering and diffusion retardation are not established.
